samples.summary: New depth cap in `normalizeYsonTreeNode` has no test at all
samples.evidence: This delta adds a `row`-counting depth cap to `normalizeYsonTreeNode` (snapshot-adapters.ts, the `if (!(isRow && depth >= MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH))` branch), justified by "a peer-written block > row > cell > block > table > … chain overflows the stack on this recursion before the capped reader ever sees it". No test exercises it: `packages/frontend/src/components/history/__tests__/snapshot-adapters.test.ts` has no reference to MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH or to any deeply nested tree (its deepest cases are the fixture table and the 4-level 'YSON parse limits' tree at line 362). A grep for MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH across the repo returns only yorkie-doc-store.test.ts, docx-importer.test.ts and table-nesting.test.ts — no history test. So neither the stack-overflow protection nor the off-by-one of counting `row` ancestors (whether this walk truncates at the same table `docsTreeToDocument` does) is pinned; a regression would only show as a crashed revision-preview tab or a silently different truncation.

No test drives a Tab press over a cyclic parent map: only two test files dispatch a 'Tab' key (`test/view/header-table-nav.test.ts`, `test/view/editor-tab-bullet.test.ts`), and neither builds a cyclic map; the existing cycle tests in `test/view/nested-table-cell-range.test.ts:334-422` cover `normalizeRange`, `Doc.findBlock` and `resolvePositionPixel` but not the editor's cell navigation. Comparable guards on this PR did get tests, so this one is an unpinned guard whose failure mode is a hard tab crash for every peer of a malformed document.

samples.summary: The merge-expansion budget test's only real assertion is wall-clock timing
samples.evidence: In 'returns promptly on a large table of orphan covered cells', the two value assertions are trivially true regardless of the budget: `out.start` equals the input start (the loop only ever *shrinks* rowStart/colStart toward 0, and the input is already 0,0) and `out.end.rowIndex >= rows-1` holds because rowEnd is initialised to rows-1 and only grows. So only `expect(elapsed).toBeLessThan(2000)` can fail — a timing assertion that is CI-load dependent and says nothing about *what* the budget does. No test asserts the documented degradation (a budget-exhausted expansion returns the partially-expanded rectangle) or that `findMergeTopLeftBudgeted` answers `(r, c)` when out of budget, so the budget's semantics are unpinned even though its speed is.
searchedFor: read the budget code in packages/docs/src/view/selection.ts

verdict.reason: The depth cap is real and reachable: snapshot-adapters.ts:150-157 drops a `row` node's children once `depth >= MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH`, with `depth` incremented only on `row` nodes, and it is exercised in production only via parseDocsSnapshot (line 195) from revision-preview.tsx:88. I read the entire test file for that module (snapshot-adapters.test.ts, 431 lines): the parseDocsSnapshot suite's deepest case is a single-level table from the fixture (lines 294-312) and the 'YSON parse limits' suite builds a 4-level tree (362-367); no test constructs a row chain approaching 32, asserts truncation, or asserts that a deep tree does not throw. The docs fixture contains only a shallow table, so no fixture-driven test can reach the cap. Searching wider: the only other importer of the module is board-preview-viewport.test.ts (parseBoardSnapshot only); revision-preview.test.tsx:135 uses a 4-level tree; a repo-wide grep for normalizeYsonTreeNode finds no test at all, and the MAX_TABLE_NESTING_DEPTH tests that do exist (packages/docs/test/model/table-nesting.test.ts, packages/docs/test/import/docx-importer.test.ts, packages/frontend/tests/app/docs/yorkie-doc-store.test.ts:3660) all cover different code paths (treeNodeToBlock, the docx importer, the live store write path), none of which runs this recursion. Notably the analogous guard in yorkie-doc-store.ts IS pinned at yorkie-doc-store.test.ts:3660-3669, confirming the snapshot-path guard is the untested one. Failure of this guard ships as either a stack-overflow-crashed revision preview or a silently different truncation than docsTreeToDocument produces — a silently weakened guard on a user-visible path, so major under this lens. No counterexample found.
